title: Biophysical EPR Using Superconducting Resonators
authors: Austin R. Gamble Jarvi, Hamid R. Mohebbi, Ishit Raval, Omari Culzac, Jack Erickson, Sameh Hegazy, Don Carkner, Andrew Wiles, David G. Cory, Troy W. Borneman
abstract: We present innovations that enable the use of superconducting resonators for high sensitivity, high bandwidth pulsed electron paramagnetic resonance (EPR) measurements on biologically relevant samples with enhanced stability and throughput. A custom-built X-band pulsed EPR spectrometer with AWG and digital IF capability generated by an FPGA was used to control a novel patterned thin film planar superconducting microstrip resonator capable of generating Rabi fields sufficient to achieve 6 ns pi/2 Gaussian pulses using a 100 W solid-state HPA. The system allows automated sequential calibration, measurement, and analysis of five 3.5 uL samples contained in a sample cartridge. Performance was validated through measurements of double electron-electron resonance (DEER) distances in a variety of spin-labeled protein samples with biologically relevant concentrations, including measurements below 10 uM. The results enable broadening the scope of applications for both superconducting resonators and the use of EPR in biotechnology.
summary: The paper details the engineering and experimental implementation of a state-of-the-art pulsed EPR spectrometer utilizing superconducting microstrip resonators. By integrating advanced pulse sequences like RDSE, the system achieves high stability and sensitivity necessary for measuring distances in multiple, small, biologically relevant samples simultaneously.
main_problem: The goal is to develop a high-sensitivity, stable, and automated Electron Paramagnetic Resonance (EPR) system capable of measuring distance distributions in biologically relevant samples using superconducting resonators.
main_result: The novel superconducting resonator design enables multi-sample measurement cartridges while achieving Signal-to-Noise Ratios (SNR) comparable to higher frequency Q-band systems, pushing biophysical EPR into more practical settings.
method: The authors employed advanced pulsed EPR techniques like Double Electron-Electron Resonance (DEER), utilizing sophisticated pulse sequences such as RDSE and CPMG echo trains for signal enhancement.
model_or_system: The core platform is a custom X-band pulsed EPR spectrometer built around a patterned thin film planar superconducting microstrip resonator. This system operates in a cryogen-free environment, allowing precise control over microwave fields to probe spin systems.
key_observables: Double electron-electron resonance (DEER) distances between paramagnetic centers, Signal-to-Noise Ratio (SNR), and Rabi pulse strengths ($\pi/2$ Gaussian pulses).
important_parameters: Operating Frequency: 9.5 GHz; Sample Volume: $3.5 \mu	ext{L}$; Superconducting material enabling operation at 50 K.
main_assumptions: The analysis sometimes neglects complex subspace structure associated with finite temperature spin ensembles (Tavis-Cummings model).
figures_summary: Figures illustrate the resonator geometry, system characterization via VNA measurements, and distance measurement results comparing various advanced pulse sequences (RDSE vs. 4p-DEER) for T4-Lysozyme.
paper_structure: The paper details the engineering innovations of the superconducting resonator setup, presents methods for automated multi-sample acquisition, validates performance using DEER on protein samples, and discusses achieving high SNR through advanced pulse sequences.
why_interesting: This work directly bridges quantum optics/AMO physics (pulsed spectroscopy, cavity QED concepts applied to resonators) with biophysics. The use of superconducting circuits to enhance sensitivity for molecular measurements is highly relevant to open quantum systems research.

figures.caption: Figure 1: Overview of superconducting resonator design. (a) Rendering of the 16-strip superconducting YBCO resonator used in this work with mode-matched sample cartridge placed in the homogeneous field region. The small size of the samples (3.5 µL) enables five sample cavities of roughly 3 mm x 2 mm x 400 µm each to be contained in a single cartridge. Adjustment of coupling into and out of the device is achieved through variation of a capacitive gap between the set of phased λ/2 resonators and a branching feedline that matches the impedance of each microstrip. Figure 2: Overview of system characterization. (a) Microscope photograph of the 2-port 16-strip 300 nm YBCO superconducting microstrip resonator structure used in this study with ports labeled. Each microstrip is 4.532 mm long and 70 µm wide with 70 µm separation between strips. The capacitive coupling gap is 60 µm for both ports. VNA S-parameter measurements show an X-band frequency of 9.447 GHz with an overcoupled Q of roughly 80, corresponding to a bandwidth of roughly 125 MHz. S11 and S22 data indicate the device is 50 Ωmatched at both ports. (b) Nutation data with Fourier transform in the inset. Figure 3: Shaped pulse RDSE distance measurement data for T4-Lysozyme. (a) Pulse sequence schematics for 4p-DEER and 3p-DEER showing the usage of Gaussian observe pulses and adiabatic pump pulses. The dipolar evolution time is incremented commensurate with 2H-ESEEM (448 ns) according to the RELOAD algorithm. The 3p-DEER and 4p-DEER measurements are stitched according to the DEER-Stitch algorithm. The detected echo is refocused periodically by a CPMG sequence to increase SNR by averaging over a train of echoes in a single acquisition.
